title: Chapter 98 – Veiled Forge
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

Five months later.

The thaw comes in the night, with a sound like a very large animal turning over in its sleep.

Jian wakes to it in the dark of his cell, and lies still, listening. Something is groaning on the ridge above the Inner Court, a long deep creak of ice giving way, and under it the quick bright chatter of water finding its old channels. A drip begins at the eave. Then another. By the time the window turns gray the whole mountain is talking, every gutter and spout and crack in the stone running with meltwater, and the smell that comes in through the shutters is the smell of wet earth and bruised pine and the first green things.

He sits up. Pebble, curled on the pillow, lifts its head.

Water, it says drowsily. Everywhere.

"The thaw."

Warm?

"Soon."

He swings his feet to the cold floor and rolls up his left sleeve. For five months the Spring Vein has lain along the inside of his arm like a length of gray cord. Every morning he has looked at it, and every morning it has been the same. Tonight he turns the arm to the window, and in the pale light a thread of green runs along the vein, no wider than a hair, from the elbow to the wrist.

He stares at it. Then he lets out a breath he did not know he was holding.

The cost of a thing is also the shape of it, he thinks. It sleeps with the year. It wakes with the year.

He lays his palm against the wet shutter, where a single blade of moss has pushed up through a seam in the wood, and draws.

* * *

The Spring Vein takes what it needs and gives a little back.

He has known that since the mountain trial. A draw once a day, from the living source nearest to hand: a patch of moss, a root, a sleeping seed. It pulls on the thing until the thing is spent, and what it pulls goes into his arm as a cool green warmth, and into the Interface as something else. The panel opens at the corner of his eye in the cold gray light.

```
SPRING VEIN — DRAW
Source: moss (1 blade). Consumed.
Yield: 1 CE.
Daily limit: 1 draw.
Cost: source destroyed. Seasonal. Dormant below freezing.
CE: 53.
```

Fifty-three. It is a good number, for him. For five months he has built it a point at a time, from nothing: a tonic mixed for Bai, a hinge repaired in the Sutra Hall, a lesson taught to Yue in the herbal room, each small task logging a point or two on the panel. The Interface had called it Operator labor, and it had not been generous. But the numbers have added up. Fifty-three CE is more than he has held since the Dock.

It is not yet sixty. It is not yet enough.

"Sixty," he says aloud to the room, and Pebble wrinkles its snout.

Sixty what?

"A key."

Key to what?

"A door in a room I have only seen once." He rolls the sleeve down. "I think it will take me to the next one."

* * *

The points do not come from nowhere. He earns them in the Pill Hall.

It is a bargain he struck with Bai in the first month, on the old man's spare cot. Rank One is Rank One, whatever tier he wears, and the Hall has always needed hands that can grind a powder fine enough to float. Two evenings a week, after Kuang's pole and Ouyang's cold breathing, Jian goes down the mountain to the hundred little furnaces and works until the lamps burn low. Bai pays him in plums, in tea, and in a silence that is worth more than either. The Interface pays him in something else.

Tonight the work is a batch of Heartroot tonic for the Outer Court's winter fevers, forty doses, to be ground, measured, and sealed in wax. He does it by feel. The pestle moves, the powder falls, and in the corner of his eye the panel counts.

```
TASK: Operator labor (alchemy). 40 doses ... complete.
Yield: 2 CE.
Weekly cap: 6 CE (labor).
```

Two points for a night. It is a miserly rate. The Interface does not pay for effort, only for difference, and the difference between a tonic ground by a clumsy hand and one ground by a careful one is small. He has long since stopped resenting it. A rate is a rate. If a man cannot afford a miracle, he can at least afford to be patient.

"You are doing that wrong," says Bai.

The old Elder has appeared at his shoulder, a plum in each fist, and is peering at the sealed doses with a critical eye.

"The wax is too thick?"

"The wax is perfect. The pestle is wrong. You grind with your wrist now. You used to grind with your shoulder." Bai bites a plum. "Foundation has changed your hand. It is lighter. The powder floats too fine. It will blow off the scale."

Jian looks at the pestle. It is true. The strokes have a new ease, a smoothness that comes from nowhere in particular. His Qi has begun to live in his hands without being asked.

"I will correct it."

"Do. And do not ask me how I know." Bai chews. "I am an old man with an excellent nose and no pulse-reading skill whatever."

It is the fifth time the old Elder has said it, in one form or another. Jian has stopped asking what he knows.

* * *

The Legacy Hall is a long gallery on the north side of the Inner Court, and it is the one place in the Sect where anyone is allowed to be disappointed.

It is a hall of lists. Black boards line the walls from floor to ceiling, hundreds of them, each painted with rows of white characters, and every character is a name, a craft, or a loss. The Sword of the Nine Rains. Lost, year 211. The Jade Bell Method. Last holder dead without a successor. The Thousand-Needle Rain. Fragments only. A hundred years of Inner Court history written in the language of what has been forgotten. The air smells of beeswax and dust. At the far end a few disciples stand in front of the boards, reading, as pilgrims read the names on a memorial.

Jian walks the length of it slowly. He has come here on Elder Ye's advice. "The Inner Court keeps a record of every craft the Sect has lost," she told him in the herbal room, weeks ago. "It is a long and depressing document. I find it clarifies the mind."

He finds the board he is looking for in the third bay.

ARTIFACT REFINING — LOST INHERITANCES

There are nine entries. He reads them one by one.

The Hundred Veins Forge Canon, Volumes 2 through 9. Burned, year 489, in the fire of the Coral Gate Forge. He has heard that one before, from Hu. The Cloudstitch Loom. Destroyed. The Nine Furnace Method. Never recorded. And at the very bottom, in a smaller hand, as if the painter had written it last and with some reluctance:

The Veiled Forge. Method of refining artifacts under concealment, so that neither the forge nor the work may be seen or sensed by any Qi-reader below the Core. Founded by an unknown master of the Coral Gate. Last known practitioner: Master Ling, died year 489. Method lost.

He stands in front of the board for a long time.

So that neither the forge nor the work may be seen. Hu's old shop. The one that burned. The forge the clan thought was a secret until the day it was not.

"Reading the dead?" says a voice at his shoulder.

He turns.

The young man who has come up beside him is tall, lean, and impeccably dressed in the silver-edged gray of a Silver Leaf, with a jade pin in his hair and a sword at his hip that is worth more than Jian's family's entire Garden. His face is handsome in a cold, carved way. His eyes are pale. He is looking at the board with the faint amusement of a man looking at a child's drawing.

"Disciple Shen," Jian says.

"You know my name."

"Everyone knows your name." It is true. Shen Yuhang is the second son of a Core-bound house, a Foundation Middle cultivator at twenty-six, and the only Silver Leaf disciple ever to have been given a personal sword by an Elder. "I have seen you in the training yard."

"You have seen me on the lists." Shen's smile does not move. "I have seen you on the lists as well. The Gate Bearer. Provisional." He gives the last word a faint, polished weight. "I was curious to see what a provisional looks like at his leisure."

"A man reading a board."

"A man reading a board of dead crafts. How appropriate." The pale eyes slide over the entries. "Artifact refining. Is that your interest? I had heard you were an alchemist's boy."

"I am curious about many things."

"Curiosity is an expensive habit in the Inner Court." Shen turns his head, finally, and looks straight at him. "You are Foundation Early, they say, at twenty-one. An impressive feat. Some people would say suspicious. I do not hold with that. I think it is simply remarkable." He pauses. "I only wonder what else you might be hiding."

The words lie between them like a coin on a table.

"I will let you know," says Jian, "when I find out."

Shen laughs. It is a short, genuine laugh, surprised out of him, and for a moment the cold carving of his face breaks and shows a human thing underneath, curious and sharp and quite unafraid. Then it closes again.

"We will speak again, Gate Bearer," he says. "I think there will be reason."

He walks away down the gallery with his sword swinging, and the other disciples part before him like water.

A rival, Jian thinks. Or the shape of one. He files it. He will need it later.

He looks once more at the board, at the last entry. The Veiled Forge. Method lost.

Then he turns, and goes to find a carter.

* * *

Old Hu comes up the mountain on the tenth day of the fourth month, on a visiting pass, with a wooden crate in his one hand and a satchel on his shoulder, and the whole Inner Court stares.

He is not made for it. The white stone gate, the swept paths, the tiers of gray and silver, all of it is a world he has no use for. He is wearing his best robe, patched in three places, and his iron arm, the wooden stump with its leather cuff, is polished like a pair of boots. He stands at the foot of the long stair with the crate at his feet and looks around at the Inner Court as a man looks at a country whose language he does not speak.

"This is a lot of stairs," he says, when Jian reaches him.

"It is a mountain."

"I know it is a mountain. I did not know it would try to kill me." He sets the satchel on the crate and wipes his forehead. "The steward asked my business. I said I was here to see the Gate Bearer, and he went white. He gave me tea. Is that normal?"

"It is not unusual."

"It is bad tea." Hu squints at him. "You look better than you did. Your mother says you were skin and bone at the stair."

"I have been fed."

"Hm." The old forge master is silent for a moment. Then he picks up the crate again and holds it out. "Here. I brought you something. It took me three days to find the box."

Jian takes the crate. It is heavy for its size. He sets it on the stone, kneels, and lifts the lid.

Inside, wrapped in oilcloth, lies a book.

It is a thin thing, bound in a plate of bone, with a cover scored by old fire. The vellum pages are brown at the edges and curled. On the front, in faded characters, three words: Hundred Veins Forge. And beneath them, smaller: Volume the First.

"I told you about it," Hu says. "In the spring. I packed it when I thought I would leave. It is the only one that survived. I carried it out of the fire inside my shirt, and the shirt burned, and the book did not." His voice has dropped. "I have read it a hundred times. I thought I understood it. I was wrong. I understand the first third, and the rest is a language I cannot read."

"A language."

"Coral Gate script. It is a trade hand, the old masters wrote it in a private cipher, and nobody alive can break it. I have tried." He sniffs. "But I thought, the boy reads things. The boy reads the Founder's marks. Perhaps he can tell me what the cipher is for."

Jian does not answer. He opens the book. The first page is a line drawing of a forge, an ordinary hearth with a bellows, and beside it a sketch of a hammer. Beneath, a paragraph in a cramped hand. He reads it silently.

He can read it.

It is not the Dock's script. It is something else, cramped, curling, built from the same strokes but in a different order, like a cousin of the Founder's language that has been left to grow in the dark. But the logic is the same. The root forms are the same. He has seen enough of the old marks that his mind fills in the gaps, and as he reads, the meaning comes up through the page like a face through water.

The Forge is not a fire. The Forge is a place where a thing is made to agree with itself. Hammer and metal and Qi are three voices; the master teaches them to sing a single note...

"Well?" says Hu.

"It is a method," he says slowly. "Of coupling. The veins in the metal, the lines of Qi in the work. It describes how to find them, and how to bring them into one."

"I knew that part."

"The rest..." He turns a page. "The rest is about concealment. About hiding the work from sensing. It says the forge must be a quiet place, a place that does not speak. It describes a veil that is woven from the work itself. It is not an array." He lifts his eyes. "Hu, this is the first step of the Veiled Forge."

The old man's face does not change. But the muscle in his jaw jumps once.

"You are certain."

"I am certain it is the first step. I do not know that I can do the rest."

"But you can read it."

"I can read it."

Hu says nothing for a long moment. Then he sits down on the stair, heavily, with his stump across his knee, and looks at the ground between his boots. When he raises his eyes there is something in them Jian has not seen before, raw and lit and a little frightened.

"I have waited thirty years to hear someone say that," he says. "Thirty years. I thought I would die first." He rubs his face with his hand. "Do you know what I would give to make one thing in that style? One. A single hammer, forged in the quiet. Just to know I had done it."

"You may get your chance."

"Do not say that to an old man unless you mean it."

"I mean it," Jian says. "I do not yet know how."

* * *

They eat in the guest hall at dusk, the four of them at a long table under a lamp: Hu, Feng, Jian, and Yue, who has been fetched from the herbal room with ink to her elbows.

The Inner Court's kitchen sends up rice, pickled greens, a dish of braised pork, a pot of tea that Hu inspects with deep suspicion. Hu eats like a man who expects to be stopped. Feng watches him with the fond impatience of a nephew. Yue eats nothing, because she is explaining the difference between silverthread and ghostmint to anyone who will listen.

"The edges," she says, tapping a drawing. "Silverthread has a saw edge. Ghostmint is smooth. And it smells wrong."

"Wrong how?" says Hu.

"Like cold metal. I do not know how else to say it."

"That is a good sign," says the old forge master, and his rough face softens. "A thing that smells of metal knows what it is." He reaches for the pork. "I have eight guards who can hold a spear. Twelve with a staff. I would like twenty with something better than iron that bends. I would like to give them each a blade that does not break the first time a Foundation man leans on it."

"Steel," says Feng.

"Real steel. The sort Mu's Pool-grade blade is made of. I cannot make it. I can only cut it." Hu looks at Jian. "I know it is a lot to ask."

"It is a lot," Jian agrees. "I will see what I can do."

"You always say that."

"And I always do something."

Hu grunts, which is agreement. He chews for a while in silence.

"The clan is seventy-one now," says Feng. "Two babies in the east kitchen. A pair of cousins from the south came last month with a cart of rice and a letter of introduction. Mother says it is a house at last, not a camp."

"I want to see it."

"Come at the new moon. You are allowed one pass a month, with Ye's signature." Feng lowers his voice. "Mother asks about the cloak. The one she made you. She says you never wear it."

Jian glances down. He is wearing the cloak now.

"I wear it every day."

"I know that. I told her." Feng smiles. "She wanted to hear it from you."

Beneath the table, a small cold paw lands on his knee. Pebble, who has been given a corner of pork and a saucer of tea, looks up at him with great seriousness.

Family, it says. Good.

He lays a hand on the animal's back, and does not reply, because there is nothing to say.

* * *

Qin Hao is at the fortieth landing when he comes, as he is every night.

The Guard is sitting on a folding stool with a blanket across his knees and a thin book in his hands, reading by the light of a paper lantern. He does not look up. He looks, Jian thinks, a little rounder than he did in the winter, a little less gray around the mouth. There is a cup of tea at his elbow, and a small bag of dried plums that Jian recognizes.

"Elder."

"Gate Bearer." Qin Hao closes the book on a finger. "You are late. It is a quarter past the second bell. The Enforcement lads have been asking whether you intend to sleep in the Dock."

"I was visiting my clan's forge master. He brought a book."

"A book." The scholar's beard twitches. "I have been wondering how long it would take you to find a reason to go down. I thought a month. You took five." He gestures at the wall with his chin. "Go on. Two hours, and I will say it was one. If anything happens, strike the stone three times."

"What would happen?"

"I have no idea. That is why I say it." He opens his book again. "Go on."

Jian hesitates. Then, because the question has been in his mind for a long while, he says: "Elder. Why did you do it? At the council. Why did you stake the name?"

Qin Hao does not answer at once. He turns a page. Then, without looking up, in a voice so quiet that the Enforcement disciples on the far stairs cannot hear:

"Because my teacher stood on this landing for eighty years and died without ever being asked to open the door. She told me on her deathbed that it was the saddest thing in her life. That she had kept a post that nobody wanted kept." He looks at the page. "I did not want to die the same way. That is all."

The lantern flickers. A moth blunders into it, falls, and gets up.

"I am glad you did," Jian says.

"So am I. Most days." The Guard waves a hand. "Go. And Lin Jian."

"Elder?"

"Whatever you bring out of there. Tell Ye first. I will pretend I did not see."

* * *

The wall opens for him as it has opened before.

The hum rises in the dark. At the foot of the long stair, in the pale round room, the bench lies where he left it, with the dust still showing the long clean outline of a body. The chair. The register. The gray hood folded in its flower.

He does not lie down. He walks past the bench, to the far side of the chamber, where a second recess in the wall lies behind a panel of smoked glass.

On his first visit he thought it was a vent. On his second, he saw that it was something else. Now he lays his palm on the glass, and it clears, and the panel flares.

```
ARK-6 / DOCK 2 — FABRICATOR
Status: DORMANT. Operator Level 1 detected.
Function: compound fabrication (Level 4 required for full use).
Test print available at Level 1: 40 CE.
Warning: test print consumes CE and returns a blank. Blank is a calibration piece only.
CE: 53.
Proceed?
```

He considers it. Forty of fifty-three. Thirteen left. The cost is plain, and it is large. For a month he will have to rebuild it. For a month his reserve will be a thin film.

But a blank is a measurement. And a measurement tells a man how far he is from the thing he needs.

"Proceed," he says.

The glass hums. A cold light pours out of the recess, and in the center of it a shape begins to form: a thin disc, then a bar, then a lattice of fine silver lines that crawl over its surface like frost on a window. It takes twenty breaths. When the light dies, a small object lies on the shelf of the recess, still faintly glowing.

He picks it up.

It is a plate the size of his palm, a blank of some dark pale metal, with a shallow groove cut across the face. The groove is a pattern. It is very fine, and very regular. He turns it to the light. It is a map of veins.

```
CALIBRATION BLANK — COMPLETE.
Pattern match against stored schematics:
"Veiled Forge" (partial) ... 31%
Missing: coupling sequence, quiet-fire profile, 3 reference veins.
Reference source: Hundred Veins Forge, vol. 1 (identified in Operator inventory? NO).
Advice: bring reference volume to bench.
Level 4 required to fabricate working components.
Level 4 requirement: 60 CE (bench synthesis unlock).
CE: 13.
```

He reads it again and again.

Reference source: Hundred Veins Forge, volume one. The bench knows the book. It has known the book for six hundred years, and has been waiting for someone to carry it in the door.

He holds the blank in his palm, a cold small weight. It is a calibration piece, nothing more. And it fits his hand perfectly.

Thirty-one percent, he thinks. A third of the way to a lost craft. And the key is a book in a crate and sixty points of energy.

Pebble clambers up his arm and sniffs the plate. Its snout wrinkles.

Forge, it says. Old forge. Quiet. Then, after a moment, very carefully, as if testing the word: Hu. Happy.

Jian closes his fingers over the blank.

"Yes," he says. "Hu will be happy."

He takes the book out of his satchel and sets it on the shelf of the fabricator, where the light can read it. The panel flickers. A line of script crawls across it, too fast to follow, and then holds steady.

```
REFERENCE VOLUME DETECTED.
Scanning... complete.
Fabrication of Veiled Forge components now possible at Level 4.
New capability pending: UNLOCK AT 60 CE.
```

On the bench behind him, in the dusty outline of his own body, a single mote of light drifts up from the metal and goes out.
